Dr. Isaiah Miguel Blankson (1944–2021) was a Ghanaian aerospace engineer, born in Cape Coast, who attended Mfantsipim School and graduated in 1964 with the highest A-Level scores in West Africa. He went on to earn his B.S., M.S., and Ph.D. in Aeronautics and Astronautics from MIT, becoming the first African to receive a doctorate in the field.

The Unifying Thread of His Work

His career was defined by the masterful use of electromagnetism and plasma to solve aerospace problems — what the document calls magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) and plasma aerodynamics. He was also a gifted lateral thinker, famously drawing inspiration from emperor penguins to devise a laser-based sonic boom suppression system.

Career Arc

He worked at Xerox's Webster Research Laboratory (1973–1982), then General Electric's Corporate Research Center (1982–1988), and finally NASA (1988–2021) — first as Generic Hypersonics Program Director at headquarters, then as Deputy Director of the Hypersonics Division, and finally as one of only 12 Senior Technologists at Glenn Research Center in Cleveland.

Key Contributions

His work helped initiate NASA's Hyper-X program, which produced the X-43A scramjet that flew at Mach 6.83 and Mach 10 in 2004. He held four patents — the Exoskeletal Gas Turbine Engine (2002), the MHD-Controlled Gas Turbine Engine (2004), a sonic boom suppression method using laser-induced plasma (2015), and a water purification system using cold plasma (2018). He also developed a millimeter-wave radiation camera for low-visibility aviation safety and weapons detection, and continued work on magnetic levitation for aerospace testing and space launches.

Legacy Beyond the Lab

He authored over 100 papers with 995 citations, mentored the next generation of scientists at multiple universities including HBCUs, helped establish a Department of Aeronautics at the University of Science and Technology in Ghana, collaborated with Moscow State University on millimeter-wave imaging research, and served as the U.S. National Delegate to NATO's Working Group on Hypersonic Vehicle Technology from 1998 until his death.

Honours

His awards spanned MIT, NASA, and the African American community — including two Presidential Rank Awards (the highest honours available to U.S. federal scientists), the NASA Exceptional Technology Achievement Medal, the AIAA Fellowship, the Black Engineer of the Year Award, and the National Emerald Honors Black Scientist of the Year. Science Spectrum Magazine famously put him on its cover in 2005 and nicknamed him the "Speed Demon" — at NASA he was also known simply as "Dr. Speed."

In One Sentence

Isaiah Miguel Blankson was one of the most brilliant, creative, and consequential aerospace engineers of his generation — a Ghanaian boy from Cape Coast who climbed one hill at Mfantsipim and spent the rest of his life conquering far greater ones.

Here is a summary of the profile of Professor Kojo Mensa-Wilmot:

Kojo entered Mfantsipim in 1969, graduating in 1976 (MOBA-74), where a chemistry teacher named Richard Snell sparked his lifelong interest in chemistry. He went on to study Biochemistry at the University of Ghana, Legon, where professors inspired his interest in organic chemistry and parasitic diseases. Academic Journey

At Johns Hopkins he completed a master's in Biochemistry, then a PhD in Molecular Biology under Roger McMacken in 1988 — becoming the first Black PhD graduate in Molecular Biology from the Bloomberg School of Public Health. He followed this with a Rockefeller Foundation postdoctoral fellowship under Paul Englund, studying the African trypanosome.

Career Achievements

Joining UGA in 1992, over nearly 30 years he discovered drug candidates for sleeping sickness, pioneered kinase scaffold repurposing, published over 80 papers, secured a $2.6 million NIH grant, was elected a Fellow of the African Academy of Sciences, and became the first Black chair of a science department at UGA.

Later Career

In 2020 he became Dean at Kennesaw State University — the first Black dean of Science and Mathematics there — securing an additional $3.3 million in NIH funding, before stepping down from the deanship to focus fully on his research.

Legacy

A trailblazer and mentor, he embodies Mfantsipim's motto
"Dwen Hwe Kan"
— Think Ahead — dedicating his career to solving health problems that afflict people in his home continent.

Distinguished Alumnus Award – Public Service and Governance

Dr John Kissi

I am honoured to nominate Dr. John Kissi for the Mfantsipim School 150th Anniversary Distinguished Alumnus Award in Public Service and Governance in recognition of his outstanding and sustained contributions to public service, institutional leadership, and disaster-resilient infrastructure at both national and international levels.

Dr. John Kissi's journey of leadership began at Mfantsipim School, where he distinguished himself not only academically but also through exceptional service and student leadership. He served as Organising Secretary of the Scripture Union, Vice President of the Preaching Group, Presidential Advisor to the Nature Fan Club, and Dining Hall President, roles that reflected his ability to unite people, inspire excellence, and serve with integrity.

He built on this strong foundation at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), where he was elected Assistant Secretary and later President of the Students' Representative Council (SRC) in 1999, earning the confidence of his peers through exemplary leadership. At every stage of his journey, Dr. Kissi has been dedicated professionally while bringing honour and distinction to his alma mater, Mfantsipim School.

For more than twenty-five years, Dr. Kissi has distinguished himself as a Chartered Civil Engineer, transformational leader, and public sector executive whose work has significantly advanced flood risk management, infrastructure resilience, and institutional governance in Ghana and internationally. As the former Director and later Chief Executive Officer of the Ghana Hydrological Authority, he successfully led the transition of the Hydrological Services Department into an autonomous Authority, became its first CEO and championed its first Ten-Year Business Development Plan. He oversaw more than fifty flood mitigation and coastal resilience projects nationwide and strengthened Ghana's flood early warning systems through strategic partnerships with national and international agencies.

His leadership extends beyond Ghana. Dr. Kissi has served as Ghana's Hydrological Advisor to the World Meteorological Organisation (WMO), Ghana’s focal person for the United Nations Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) and represented Ghana and Africa on the Executive Council of the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI), contributing to global policy on resilient infrastructure and disaster risk reduction.

Prior to returning to Ghana, Dr. Kissi built an exceptional career in the United Kingdom, leading award-winning flood alleviation and sustainable drainage projects in London, including the nationally acclaimed Herne Hill Flood Alleviation Scheme, recognised by the British Construction Industry, the Institution of Civil Engineers, and the Environment Agency. Other award-winning projects include the Salisbury Row Neighbourhood Project and the Chiswick High Road Bus Priority Project, all in London. His leadership of the team responsible for the installation of commemorative plaques across Southwark Council in London to mark Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II's Diamond Jubilee was widely recognised and in acknowledgement of the project's significance, he was invited to the official launch event at Buckingham Palace.

Beyond public office, Dr. Kissi is the Founder & CEO of Kerdos Consult, a consultancy specialising in disaster-resilient infrastructure, and the Founder & President of the Foundation for Leadership Excellence (FLEX), through which he has convened youth empowerment and leadership conferences across several countries. His passion for developing future leaders is further reflected in the X-Factor Career System, a practical career and leadership development framework born from decades of mentoring professionals and demonstrating that career success is built through intentional learning, leadership, and excellence rather than luck or circumstance, which will be launched soon.

These formative experiences shaped a leadership philosophy centred on service, excellence, integrity, and impact values that have defined his distinguished career and impact across Ghana, the United Kingdom, Canada, South Africa, the United States, and other international platforms.

Dr. John Kissi's distinguished career, unwavering integrity, visionary leadership, and enduring commitment to public service exemplify the values of Mfantsipim School. His contributions have strengthened institutions, influenced national and international policy, inspired future leaders, and improved community resilience.

He is eminently deserving of the Distinguished Alumnus Award in Public Service and Governance.

justification:
Mr. Alex Apau Dadey is a distinguished Ghanaian statesman whose more than three decades of professional and public engagement have been defined by a sustained commitment to institution-building, good governance, investment promotion, national development and service to future generations. His leadership reflects a conviction that meaningful national progress is achieved when enduring institutions, visionary leadership and productive partnerships are deliberately built and strengthened.

A defining chapter of his public-service record was his tenure as Board Chairman of the Ghana Investment Promotion Centre (GIPC) from November 2021 to January 2025. In this role, he brought extensive international and private-sector experience to a critical national institution responsible for promoting investment and strengthening Ghana's investment environment. His leadership focused on advancing an enabling environment for private-sector participation, investment attraction and economic development, while encouraging stronger collaboration between government and business.  His commitment to public service, however, extends beyond formal institutional appointments. Mr Dadey has been a strong advocate for good governance, accountable leadership and the development of institutions capable of delivering sustainable national prosperity. He has consistently argued that nations do not achieve lasting prosperity simply through natural resources or population but by building strong institutions and competitive enterprises capable of creating value and competing successfully in the global economy.

Central to his philosophy is his belief that “leadership is Africa’s most important infrastructure.” He maintains that while physical infrastructure creates opportunity, leadership determines whether that opportunity is converted into productivity, competitiveness and long-term prosperity. His advocacy therefore extends beyond leadership as a personal quality to leadership as a responsibility to build systems, strengthen institutions and create conditions in which future generations can thrive.

Mr. Dadey has also made a significant contribution to Ghana’s diaspora and investment agenda. He initiated the Ghana Diaspora Homecoming Summit in 2017 and the Ghana Investment and Opportunities Summit UK in 2018, creating platforms that connected Ghana to its global diaspora, international expertise, investment and commercial opportunities. His longstanding position is that the African diaspora remains one of the continent’s most underutilised assets and that deliberate, meaningful pathways must be created to harness its knowledge, capital, experience and influence for national and continental development.

His understanding of governance is equally grounded in trust and responsibility. He has described governance as “the currency of trust,” emphasising transparency, accountability, ethical leadership and the responsible deployment of capital as essential to building institutions that command public confidence and deliver lasting value.

His service has also extended to initiatives of national and social significance, including support for Ghana’s Black Stars and youth football development, reflecting his belief that national development encompasses not only economic progress but also the institutions, platforms and opportunities that strengthen national identity and empower young people.

His record demonstrates a consistent philosophy of service: to strengthen institutions, promote responsible leadership, connect Ghana to global opportunities and build with the interests of future generations in pursuit of a more prosperous and well-governed Ghana.

What makes KGL’s contribution particularly significant is the spirit behind the partnership. Through Executive Chairman Alex Apau Dadey, himself a proud Mfantsipim alumnus, the Group has transformed personal connection into purposeful impact—giving back to an institution that has helped shape generations of Ghanaian leaders. KGL’s role in the 150th Anniversary is therefore not simply about helping to mark a historic milestone; it is about helping Mfantsipim move confidently from a celebrated past into an even more impactful future. At a time when the anniversary calls for collective responsibility to preserve the school’s heritage and renew its infrastructure, KGL has demonstrated what it means for corporate Ghana to stand behind institutions that contribute to national development.

Ultimately, KGL Group represents the true meaning of a Partner of Impact: a partner whose contribution is measured not only by what it gives, but by what that support makes possible. Its engagement with Mfantsipim reflects a belief that investing in education, sports, mentorship and young people is an investment in Ghana itself. KGL is helping to ensure that the legacy celebrated at 150 does not remain a memory, but becomes a foundation upon which the next generation can learn, excel, lead and serve.
He has students development at heart

award_category: Distinguished Alumnus Public Service and Governance
justification:
Nomination of Mr. Frank Ivan Adama Tackie by MOBA ’67

For Public Service and Governance Award: Service to Mfantsipim School

We wish to nominate Mr. Frank Ivan Adama Tackie of the MOBA ’67 Year Group for conceiving and championing the Mfantsipim Renaissance. This structured development framework redirected projects towards Mfantsipim’s real priorities and long-term needs.

The idea had been on his mind since 1996, when he first identified an existential threat to the school. With the eye of a development planner, he observed shrinking buildable land, encroachment on school property, incomplete perimeter demarcation, fragmented land use, and projects that were often disconnected from the school’s most urgent needs.

His first attempt to address these issues came in 1996, when MOBA ’67 sought to develop a master plan as its 1997 Speech Day contribution. Although that effort was abandoned due to limited interest and cooperation at the time, the idea was revived in 2006 with the full support of the ’67 Year Group. Frank Tackie then drew on his skills in urban design and infrastructure planning, as well as the multidisciplinary capacity of his consultancy firm, to prepare the Mfantsipim Renaissance Plan for presentation at the 2007 Speech and Prize-Giving Day.

The plan was prepared without financial support from MOBA or the Church. It introduced a land-use framework that organised the school into academic, student welfare, teacher welfare, and sports zones; provided coordination for selecting and funding projects; encouraged pooled support from sponsoring Year Groups for larger initiatives; and promoted a maintenance agenda.

The initiative brought the four sponsoring Year Groups together around one coordinated programme, replacing scattered projects with projects aligned to a shared Master Plan agreed by MOBA National and the relevant authorities. Despite resistance and threats of boycott, MOBA ’67 and ’77 piloted the initiative in 2007 by tackling the abandoned six-storey complex.

Two outstanding projects emerged from the Renaissance. The first was the furnishing of the Kofi Annan Centre. It provided a new library, additional academic space, a staff common room, an examination coordination space, provision for a MOBA secretariat, a bookshop, a Maths and Science Quiz room, and a small crèche for teachers. The second was the Mfantsipim Centre for Sports Excellence, which has since attracted sustained funding and become an iconic project.

Mr. Tackie’s leadership led MOBA National to appoint him as Lead for Development Projects at the school. MOBA, the Church, and other stakeholders have since supported implementation, and the Renaissance model has largely become the blueprint for MOBA projects, although the plan is now due for renewal in light of the school’s limited land capacity and the need for substantial, coordinated funding.

Mr. Tackie also acknowledges the personal support of Messrs. James K. Morgan and Eugene Kwakye, both of MOBA ’77, for logistics and helping persuade Year Groups to embrace the Plan.

We say Ayekoo to Mr. Frank Ivan Adama Tackie for initiating this Renaissance Plan and thus making an outstanding contribution to the development of our beloved Alma Mater.

nominee_name: Pratt Oduro Abrokwa - President Moba USA
justification:
Pratt,  through sheer determination and willpower, brought a few guys together to formally launch the USA branch of Moba. He has been instrumental in the launching of the Endowment fund and provided leadership in the USA. He is tireless in  promoting  Mfantsipim and despite the distances in the USA has always tried to reach other members in the West and East Coats of America.

He is deserving of recognition for his outstanding leadership and dedication to the Moba Agenda.
He is a gifted leader

I am pleased to nominate Mr. Pratt Abrokwa for the MOBA Fraternity Award in recognition of his visionary leadership, steadfast commitment, and exceptional service as President of MOBA USA.

Under his leadership, MOBA USA has pursued an ambitious and enduring goal: the establishment of a US$1 million endowment fund to support Mfantsipim School. This initiative reflects more than a fundraising objective. It demonstrates Pratt’s determination to build a sustainable financial foundation through which generations of Old Boys can contribute to the continued development and excellence of our alma mater.

Pratt has worked tirelessly to mobilize the MOBA fraternity around this vision. He has used online forums, including WhatsApp and Facebook, to strengthen communication, encourage participation, and keep members connected to the mission. He has also organized events and fundraising activities, promoted the payment of regular dues, and consistently reminded members of their collective responsibility to Mfantsipim.

His leadership has been especially commendable because the journey has not always been easy. There have been challenges, setbacks, and occasions when anticipated goals were not achieved. Yet Pratt has never lost hope, abandoned the vision, or allowed temporary disappointments to weaken his focus. Instead, he has continued to inspire participation, maintain momentum, and encourage members to see what can be accomplished through unity, perseverance, and shared purpose.

True leadership is revealed not only when progress comes easily, but also in the ability to remain committed when results take longer than expected. Pratt has demonstrated this quality repeatedly. His resilience has helped sustain confidence in the endowment initiative and has kept the long-term interests of Mfantsipim at the centre of MOBA USA’s activities.

Pratt Abrokwa embodies the spirit of the MOBA fraternity: brotherhood, service, loyalty, sacrifice, and an unwavering commitment to advancing the welfare of Mfantsipim School. Through his vision, he has challenged Old Boys to think beyond short-term contributions and work toward building a lasting legacy for future generations.

For his visionary leadership, his dedication to mobilizing the MOBA community, and his persistent pursuit of a sustainable US$1 million endowment fund for Mfantsipim School, I strongly and wholeheartedly recommend Mr. Pratt Abrokwa for the MOBA Fraternity Award.
Pratt, leading his team, has steered the US group through thick and thin. We wouldn't have been where we're without his leadership.
He and his team have sacrificially served the MOBA USA for years.

Rev Morrison of MOBA '72 has devoted his life to a career of Education in Ghana in various positions and has left his footprint across the length and breadth of Ghana. From Kwabotwe to rural Ashanti via Salt pond and Winneba he continues to make impact on education and moral guidance of Ghanaian Youth and the Methodist Church.

He is a founding member of the MOBA USA chapter. Gathered brothers together to start the group, and was  elected its first president. Works tirelessly to organize programs that bring people together, raise funds for the chapter and for Kwabotwe . Under his leadership, the initiative for the Mfantsipim endowment has taken off . He is a great l;eader, and he has placed MOBA USA on the map, both here in the USA and globally as well.

Dr Donkor is a UN lnternational Expert and Consultant. He's led UN teams to work on water bodies such as the Nile, Congo and the Volta basins and consulted for Governments in South Africa, South Sudan, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Republic of Congo, and Ghana, among others for over thirty years.  He's also been a UN Consultant and. Expert on WASH for several countries. He's currently an International Consultant on Water and River Basins, based in Accra. He's a member of the MOBA 1972 Class.

Dr. Edwin Theophilus Coleman is an accomplished legal scholar, researcher, educator, and thought leader whose work in employment jurisprudence, constitutional rights, labour law, and legal education exemplifies academic excellence and meaningful professional impact.

Holding a Doctor of Laws (LLD) from the University of Johannesburg and having undertaken advanced studies at The Hague Academy of International Law, Dr. Coleman has established himself as a respected voice in contemporary African labour law and governance.

His scholarly contribution is particularly distinguished by his co-authorship of Labour Law in Ghana (LexisNexis, 2022), a major legal reference work examining Ghana’s statutory labour framework, employment protection, collective bargaining, and occupational health standards within an international context. His wider research interests encompass constitutional rights, free-market dynamics, labour policy, and workplace dispute resolution, with his scholarship contributing to broader legal and policy discourse.

Dr. Coleman’s academic career includes service as a Senior Postdoctoral Research Fellow at the Centre for International and Comparative Labour and Social Security Law (CICLASS) and as a lecturer at the Faculty of Law, University of Johannesburg. His international professional experience also includes work as a Legal and Research Intern at the Permanent Bureau of The Hague Conference on Private International Law in the Netherlands.

Beyond the university environment, Dr. Coleman has demonstrated a strong commitment to translating scholarship into public discourse and policy. He founded the Labour Law Society of Ghana and has served as a thought leader with the Africa Free Market Institute, contributing to national conversations on gig-economy worker protections, labour reforms, employment relations, and human rights.

His work reflects a rare combination of academic scholarship, research excellence, professional leadership, and public intellectual engagement. Through his research, teaching, institution-building, and mentorship, Dr. Coleman continues to contribute to the development of legal scholarship and the advancement of the next generation of legal professionals.

Dr. Coleman embodies the Dwen Hwɛ Kan philosophy—think and look ahead—through his commitment to advancing knowledge, shaping legal thought, and contributing to the future of Ghanaian and African labour law.

For his distinguished academic record, significant research contributions, professional leadership, and impact on legal education and public policy, Dr. Edwin Theophilus Coleman is highly deserving of recognition as a Distinguished Alumnus in Academia and Research.

award_category: Distinguished Alumnus Public Service and Governance
justification:
Osman Abdulai Ayariga (Arc. Esq.) is a distinguished lawyer, chartered architect, public administrator, and youth advocate whose career demonstrates a sustained commitment to public service, civic leadership, youth empowerment, and institutional development. As Chief Executive Officer of the National Youth Authority (NYA), he represents a compelling example of multidisciplinary leadership applied to national development.

His leadership journey was shaped early through student governance, culminating in his service as President of the National Union of Ghana Students (NUGS). In that capacity, he advocated for student welfare, equitable access to education, and greater youth participation in national affairs. His subsequent professional development reflects an exceptional breadth of expertise: he was called to the Ghana Bar in 2023 and subsequently inducted as a Chartered Architect by the Architects Registration Council and Ghana Institute of Architects in 2024.

His public and political leadership has also included service as Deputy National Youth Organizer of the National Democratic Congress (NDC), where he championed issues including youth inclusion in decision-making, fiscal accountability, transparency, and anti-corruption.

As Chief Executive Officer of the National Youth Authority, Ayariga has brought his multidisciplinary experience to the national youth development agenda. His priorities have included strengthening pathways to employment and entrepreneurship, expanding opportunities under the National Apprenticeship Programme, developing youth leadership initiatives, and pursuing partnerships that enhance technical, vocational, and professional skills development.

Beyond programmes and institutions, Ayariga has consistently advocated for non-partisan youth engagement, encouraging young people, student leaders, and emerging professionals to place service, national cohesion, leadership development, and capacity building at the centre of their contribution to Ghana.

His career stands out for the unusual combination of legal expertise, architectural training, student leadership, political engagement, and public administration. Through these experiences, he has demonstrated an ability to connect professional knowledge with public-sector leadership and the practical challenges facing Ghana’s young population.

Osman Abdulai Ayariga embodies the Dwen Hwɛ Kan philosophy through his forward-looking approach to youth development, governance, and national service. His record of leadership and commitment to empowering the next generation makes him a strong candidate for the Distinguished Alumnus – Public Service and Governance Award.

Derrick Yiiyi Annoh is an accomplished entrepreneur, business executive, and Founder and CEO of Sparkxx Foods & Beverages, whose entrepreneurial journey exemplifies innovation, resilience, local industrialization, and value-chain development within Ghana’s fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) and food-processing sector.

A graduate of the University of Ghana with a B.A. in Psychology (2012), Derrick founded Sparkxx Foods in 2014, starting modestly from his mother’s kitchen. Through experimentation, disciplined product development, rigorous quality standards, and a strong understanding of consumer needs, he transformed a small-scale home operation into a growing Ghanaian consumer brand with an expanding market presence.

Under his leadership, Sparkxx Foods has progressed from neighbourhood-level distribution to placement in major retail outlets across Ghana, while also developing pathways into international markets. His journey demonstrates how locally conceived and produced products can be developed into commercially viable brands capable of competing beyond Ghana’s borders.

Derrick’s entrepreneurial achievements have attracted notable industry recognition. In 2019, he was named a Vodafone SME Ghana Awards (SMEGA) winner, subsequently participating in executive training through the Vodafone SME Masterclass at the China Europe International Business School (CEIBS). Sparkxx Foods was also featured in the Government of Ghana’s “Amplified” initiative, highlighting innovative, high-growth Ghanaian enterprises contributing to economic development.

Beyond his own commercial achievements, Derrick represents a generation of Ghanaian entrepreneurs committed to building businesses around local production and creating value within Ghana’s economy. He advocates for youth entrepreneurship and frequently shares practical lessons with aspiring founders on brand building, local sourcing, product consistency, customer orientation, and the perseverance required to scale a business sustainably.

His entrepreneurial journey—from producing from a family kitchen to building a recognized FMCG brand with international ambitions—is a powerful demonstration of what vision, innovation, discipline, and persistence can achieve.

Derrick Yiiyi Annoh embodies the Dwen Hwɛ Kan philosophy by not merely envisioning a future of Ghanaian enterprise, but actively building it. His contribution to entrepreneurship, local manufacturing, and youth enterprise development makes him a strong candidate for the Distinguished Alumnus – Business and Entrepreneurship Award.

Sarpei Kwadey, popularly known as “Bankyehene,” is an agricultural entrepreneur, innovator, and business executive whose work demonstrates how technology, commercial enterprise, and agricultural innovation can be harnessed to transform Ghana’s food and agribusiness sector. Through his leadership in the cassava value chain, he has championed a model of agriculture that moves beyond primary production toward value addition, industrial processing, rural employment, and wealth creation.

A BSc Computer Science graduate of KNUST, Sarpei has applied systems thinking and analytical problem-solving to some of the structural challenges confronting Ghanaian agriculture. His early commitment to sustainable farming and organic food production led to the establishment of Good Food Farms, through which he sought to promote healthier soils, responsible production practices, and reduced dependence on excessive agrochemical use.

Recognising the significant economic potential of root crops, particularly cassava, Sarpei subsequently established Bankyekrom Limited, where he serves as Chief Executive Officer. Under his leadership, the company has pursued commercial-scale cassava cultivation, value addition, and processing, while contributing to rural employment and creating stronger linkages between farmers and industrial markets. His work addresses critical challenges including post-harvest losses, market access, and the need to increase the proportion of Ghanaian agricultural output that is processed locally.

Sarpei’s contribution extends beyond his own enterprises to sector-wide advocacy and industrial development. Through his engagement with the Ghana Industrial Cassava Stakeholder Platform (GICSP), he has contributed to conversations around mechanisation, improved high-starch cassava varieties, financing, processing capacity, and the development of a more competitive cassava industry. His engagement with institutions and stakeholders including GIRSAL and Development Bank Ghana reflects his commitment to creating the financial and industrial ecosystem necessary to unlock agriculture’s full economic potential.

His advocacy has also highlighted the considerable opportunity for Ghana to expand domestic processing of cassava into higher-value products such as industrial starch and ethanol, thereby reducing import dependence, strengthening local manufacturing, and retaining more value within the Ghanaian economy.

What distinguishes Sarpei Kwadey is the combination of entrepreneurial execution, agricultural innovation, sector advocacy, and a commitment to rural economic development. His work demonstrates that agriculture can be positioned not simply as subsistence activity, but as a sophisticated industrial value chain capable of generating employment, supporting farmers, stimulating manufacturing, and contributing to national economic transformation.

Sarpei Kwadey embodies the Dwen Hwɛ Kan philosophy by looking beyond conventional agricultural models and actively building pathways toward a more productive, resilient, and industrialised Ghanaian agricultural economy.

For his entrepreneurial leadership, contribution to agricultural industrialisation, innovation in the cassava value chain, and commitment to rural wealth creation, Sarpei Kwadey is strongly deserving of consideration for the Distinguished Alumnus – Business and Entrepreneurship Award.

Jesse Roland Prah is an accomplished agribusiness executive, sustainable farming advocate, and Founder and CEO of Jesse Prah Enterprise, producers of Roland Rice. A graduate of the University of Education, Winneba, Roland has transformed an unexpected career transition into a thriving agribusiness venture, demonstrating the potential of Ghanaian agriculture to create commercially viable enterprises, employment, and local value.

Following his national service, Roland began with a modest plot of farmland and steadily expanded his operations to approximately 300–400 acres in the Shama District of the Western Region. His enterprise has developed beyond cultivation into an integrated rice value chain encompassing farming, milling, destoning, polishing, packaging, and distribution. Roland Rice has subsequently reached consumers across the Western, Greater Accra, Ashanti, and Volta Regions, strengthening the market for locally produced rice.

His commitment to agricultural excellence earned early recognition when he was adjudged Best Rice Farmer in the Shama District in 2018. Beyond his own production, Roland has advocated for improved farming practices and productivity-enhancing approaches, including double-track rice cultivation, helping to promote more efficient use of available farmland among local farmers.

Roland’s entrepreneurial vision extends beyond production to sustainability and circular-economy innovation. Through his participation in the European Union-funded Boosting Green Employment and Enterprise Opportunities in Ghana (GrEEn) project, he won the inaugural GrEEn Innovation Challenge matching grant of GH¢175,000. The funding supported the establishment of a modern rice-processing facility at Anto in the Shama District, significantly strengthening his enterprise’s capacity for local value addition.

Importantly, the facility incorporates an innovative approach to agricultural waste management by converting rice husks into clean-energy fuel pellets and briquettes, providing an environmentally responsible alternative to traditional wood charcoal. This demonstrates how agricultural waste can be transformed from an environmental challenge into an additional economic resource.

His entrepreneurial and operational achievements were further recognised when Roland Rice was named Overall Best SME at the EU GrEEn Project close-out awards.

Jesse Roland Prah’s journey represents much more than the growth of a rice business. It demonstrates how local production, value addition, sustainable manufacturing, innovation, and entrepreneurship can work together to strengthen Ghana’s food security and reduce dependence on imported food products.

Through his commitment to building a commercially sustainable local rice industry while incorporating environmentally responsible production practices, Jesse Roland Prah embodies the Dwen Hwɛ Kan philosophy—looking beyond the present to build a more self-reliant, productive, and sustainable Ghana.

For his entrepreneurial achievement, contribution to local rice production and value addition, commitment to sustainable agro-processing, and role in advancing Ghanaian agribusiness, Jesse Roland Prah is strongly deserving of consideration for the Distinguished Alumnus – Business and Entrepreneurship Award.

Gideon Dendzo, popularly known as Giddens, is a creative entrepreneur, circular economy advocate, and the Founder and CEO of Giddins Ghana Limited (Giddins Innove). What began as a university-based startup has grown into a socially conscious Ghanaian fashion and eco-manufacturing enterprise specializing in high-quality leather footwear, corporate bags, and lifestyle accessories.

Gideon’s entrepreneurial journey was shaped by an early commitment to innovation and sustainability. While at university, he identified an environmental challenge in industrial manufacturing—the routine disposal of used rubber conveyor belts—and transformed this waste material into durable shoe soles. This simple but innovative idea laid the foundation for a business model that combines commercial enterprise with environmental responsibility. Today, Giddins Innove incorporates sustainable practices throughout its production processes while maintaining a strong business-to-business (B2B) focus, supplying customized conference bags, corporate laptop bags, artisanal footwear, and other products to major local and international organizations.

A graduate of the Dutch-sponsored Orange Corners Ghana incubator, Gideon has demonstrated the ability to translate entrepreneurial opportunity into sustainable business growth. He successfully leveraged Orange Corners Innovation Fund (OCIF) financing to expand factory operations, acquire specialized production machinery, strengthen manufacturing capacity, and pursue international market opportunities. His growth trajectory has also enabled Giddins Innove to enter European markets and secure strategic retail placement at Kotoka International Airport, giving Ghanaian-made products greater visibility among both domestic and international consumers.

Gideon’s contribution extends beyond business growth to meaningful social impact. At the heart of Giddins Innove’s model is the recruitment, training, and employment of vulnerable young people and school dropouts. Through practical, technical, and vocational training, the enterprise equips young people with marketable skills and opportunities to build dignified and sustainable livelihoods. In this regard, Gideon demonstrates that entrepreneurship can serve not only as a vehicle for wealth creation but also as a mechanism for skills development, social inclusion, and youth empowerment.

His influence also extends to the development of Ghana’s industrial standards and manufacturing ecosystem. Gideon serves on the Technical Committee of the Ghana Standards Authority (GSA) for Leather and Leather Products, contributing industry expertise to the development of national quality standards and regulatory frameworks for Ghana’s emerging leather and leather-products sector. His participation reflects the growing recognition of his expertise and positions him as a practitioner contributing directly to the formalization and advancement of an important local manufacturing industry.

Gideon Dendzo’s story embodies the spirit of Mfantsipim’s creed of  thinking and looking  ahead. From transforming industrial waste into useful products, to building a competitive Ghanaian manufacturing enterprise, creating opportunities for vulnerable youth, expanding Ghanaian products into international markets, and contributing to national standards development, he has demonstrated the vision, resilience, innovation, and sense of responsibility expected of a distinguished alumnus.

His achievements represent more than personal entrepreneurial success; they demonstrate how innovation, sustainability, local manufacturing, skills development, and social responsibility can converge to create lasting economic value. For his pioneering contribution to sustainable enterprise, youth empowerment, Ghanaian manufacturing, and the development of the leather industry, Gideon Dendzo is highly deserving of recognition as a Distinguished Alumnus in Business and Entrepreneurship.

Dr. Eric Tetteh Ayertey is a distinguished sports and exercise medicine specialist, medical officer, and researcher whose pioneering contributions to athlete healthcare, anti-doping, injury prevention, and sports science have strengthened the standards of sports medicine in Ghana and beyond. His work reflects a rare combination of clinical expertise, scientific research, sports governance, and international service.

Dr. Ayertey holds a Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery (MBChB) from the University of Ghana Medical School and an MSc in Sport and Exercise Sciences from Loughborough University, United Kingdom. This multidisciplinary training enables him to bridge clinical medicine and advanced sports science, applying evidence-based approaches to athlete health, performance, injury prevention, and long-term wellbeing.

As a prominent member of the Ghana Football Association (GFA) Medical Committee, Dr. Ayertey contributes to critical areas of football medical governance and athlete welfare. His responsibilities and expertise encompass Pre-Participation Medical Evaluations (PPMEs), workload monitoring, overuse injury prevention and management, clinical governance, and anti-doping education. Through his engagement with Premier League clubs and youth development programmes, he contributes to building stronger medical systems and promoting a culture of athlete safety from grassroots to elite competition.

His professional credentials and international affiliations further distinguish his contribution. Dr. Ayertey has undertaken training and certification associated with FIFA, the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA), and the International Olympic Committee (IOC), and serves as an internationally accredited doping control officer and sports cardiology specialist. Through these roles, he contributes to the global effort to protect the integrity of sport while ensuring that athletes receive appropriate medical care and support.

Dr. Ayertey’s expertise has also been recognized on major international sporting platforms. He served on the frontline medical and anti-doping teams for the 2023 African Games, contributing to the health, safety, and integrity of athletes competing at a major continental sporting event. He was subsequently selected as an International Athlete Support Delegate and member of the medical workforce for the Paris 2024 Olympic and Paralympic Games, placing him among the professionals entrusted with supporting athletes at the highest level of international sport.

His contribution extends beyond football and athletics. Dr. Ayertey is an accredited ringside physician working with the Ghana Boxing Authority, where his expertise contributes to the protection of boxers in a high-risk contact sport. His research into Bukom boxing concussion injuries further demonstrates his commitment to addressing health challenges specific to African athletes. This research was presented at the IOC Conference on Illness and Injury Prevention in Monaco, providing an international platform for Ghanaian research and highlighting the importance of athlete-health issues within African sporting communities.

What distinguishes Dr. Ayertey is the breadth and impact of his contribution. He operates at the intersection of medicine, sports science, athlete safety, research, anti-doping, and sports administration, helping to move Ghanaian sports medicine from reactive treatment toward prevention, evidence-based practice, and comprehensive athlete welfare.

Through his dedication to clean sport, scientific research, injury prevention, clinical excellence, and elite athlete safety, Dr. Eric Tetteh Ayertey exemplifies the Dwen Hwe Kan ethos. His work not only protects athletes competing today but also contributes to building stronger medical systems and healthier sporting careers for the next generation.

For his outstanding contribution to sports medicine, athlete welfare, anti-doping, sports research, and the advancement of Ghanaian expertise on international sporting platforms, Dr. Eric Tetteh Ayertey is highly deserving of the Sports Excellence Award.

Gideon Quagraine is a distinguished insurance executive and financial risk specialist whose career has contributed to the growth of insurance solutions, corporate risk management, and financial resilience in Ghana. Through his analytical and strategic approach to risk mitigation, financial planning, and corporate insurance underwriting, he has helped organizations and individuals better understand, manage, and protect against financial uncertainty.

Throughout his professional career in the insurance and risk management sector, Gideon has focused on developing and implementing client-centred insurance solutions that respond to the evolving needs of Ghanaian businesses and individuals. His expertise spans corporate risk advisory, asset protection, underwriting, claims management, and the development of strategies designed to protect businesses and individuals against unforeseen financial losses.

A significant aspect of his contribution has been his emphasis on making insurance more relevant and accessible to the wider Ghanaian population. By promoting greater understanding of insurance as a tool for long-term wealth preservation, business continuity, and financial security, Gideon has contributed to addressing the persistent gap between insurance products and public understanding of their value.

His professional interests also extend to the modernization of insurance practices. Gideon has advocated for the integration of micro-insurance, digital claims processing, improved customer experience, and stronger regulatory compliance within underwriting and claims-management systems. These efforts reflect an understanding that the future of insurance depends not only on the products offered but also on the accessibility, transparency, efficiency, and trustworthiness of the systems through which those products are delivered.

Beyond technical competence, Gideon’s career is distinguished by a commitment to ethical corporate governance and responsible risk management. By promoting transparency, accountability, and sound underwriting practices, he has contributed to strengthening confidence in insurance as an essential component of Ghana’s financial ecosystem. His approach recognizes that effective risk management is not merely about responding to losses after they occur, but about anticipating vulnerabilities and putting appropriate safeguards in place before risks materialize.

His contribution is particularly relevant to Ghana’s broader economic development. In an economy where businesses, households, and institutions remain vulnerable to significant financial shocks, effective insurance and risk-management systems are essential for protecting productive assets, sustaining enterprises, preserving wealth, and promoting long-term economic stability. Gideon’s work within this field therefore extends beyond individual corporate responsibilities to a broader contribution to financial resilience.

It is with great pride that I nominate Kofi Duku, an old boy of Mfantsipim School, Class of 2007, for the Mfantsipim @150 Award in the category of Environmental Sustainability, in recognition of his sustained and impactful contribution to safe water access and environmental stewardship in Ghana.

Background

Kofi currently serves as Director of Expansions and Service Delivery (previously Director of Water Quality and Service Delivery) at Saha Global, a Ghana-based non-profit that has, since 2009, trained over 1,200 women to launch and run community water treatment centers, delivering safe drinking water to more than 134,000 people across 460 villages in the Northern, Savannah, Oti, and North East Regions of Ghana. He built on a foundation of geoscience training — a B.Sc. in Geology/Earth Science from the University of Ghana, Legon — and hands-on experience as a Regional Hydrogeologist and Water Systems Engineer at the Community Water and Sanitation Agency, before joining Saha Global in 2023.

Contributions to Environmental Sustainability

1. Protecting water quality at the source. Kofi led detailed water quality analysis comparing seasonal (dry and wet) water testing data across Saha-served communities, identifying instances of cadmium exceedance traced to alum overdosing and low pH in treatment processes. Rather than treating this as an isolated technical fix, he developed soda ash dosing protocols and operator-facing job aids to correct the underlying chemistry — directly reducing the risk of heavy-metal contamination entering the water supply, and building in follow-up sampling protocols to sustain the improvement over time. He also leads the Service delivery team that ensures the continuous functionality of the over 460 water centers in the last mile areas. In Saha’s new venture into Groundwater Service Delivery in the Upper-East region. Kofi leads the team in expanding to new areas. There are a total of 534 boreholes under his management.

2. Institutionalizing safe treatment practice. He authored a borehole chlorination SOP with a rigorous dose-calculation methodology, translating technical water-safety standards into field-ready guidance that rural, community-based operators — many with limited formal technical training — can apply consistently for use at Saha in making access to clean  water in lastmile communities possible. This work embeds environmentally sound water treatment practice into the daily operations of hundreds of community water centers, rather than leaving it dependent on centralized expert oversight.

3. Sustaining performance across an expanding network. As Saha Global's model scales into new districts, Kofi developed a Performance Improvement Plan framework for operators falling below key service thresholds, helping ensure that growth in the number of served communities does not come at the cost of water quality or environmental compliance.

4. Extending impact through private-sector water engineering. Beyond his non-profit work, Kofi serves as Partner at Bueno Limited and  Hydrozone Ghana Limited, where he has led various consultancy work on borehole-fed water treatment plants, including preventive maintenance programmes addressing borehole redevelopment and iron control — extending responsible groundwater resource management into Ghana's private sector.

5. On-the-ground environmental advocacy. In his fieldwork across the Northern, North East,  Upper-East, Savannah, and Oti regions, Kofi has been a vocal advocate for site-specific sanitation strategies, publicly raising concerns about open defecation, littering, and farming practices near water sources as contamination risks — pushing local government partners toward updated Water Safety Plans.

Why This Merits Recognition

Kofi's work sits at the intersection of technical rigor and grassroots delivery: he does not merely design water-safety standards on paper, but ensures they are executable by community operators in some of Ghana's most underserved regions. His interventions — correcting contamination sources, standardizing safe chlorination, and safeguarding groundwater resources — represent exactly the kind of applied, sustained environmental stewardship that protects both public health and Ghana's water resources for the long term.

As a product of Mfantsipim School and a former Dispensary Prefect, Kofi exemplifies the institution's ethos of disciplined, purposeful service. His nomination for the Environmental Sustainability category reflects a body of work that has measurably improved water safety and environmental outcomes for well over 100,000 Ghanaians.

This award recognises not only his professional achievements, but his enduring commitment to improving cardiac health outcomes for communities across Africa and beyond.

Dr. Daniel Fiifi Tawia Hagan is an exceptional scientist whose career demonstrates how advanced science, technology, and innovation can be harnessed to address some of the defining challenges of our time—climate change, water insecurity, food security, and environmental resilience. His work sits at the intersection of hydro-climate science, satellite Earth observation, data science, climate modelling, and artificial intelligence, with a particular emphasis on developing new methods and tools for understanding and predicting climate extremes.

Dr. Hagan has established an impressive international research profile, currently serving as a Senior Research Scientist at Ghent University while collaborating with leading institutions including the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) in the United States and research teams across Europe, North America, and Asia. His research has produced more than 80 SCI-indexed publications and includes work published in highly regarded scientific journals such as Nature Communications, Scientific Data, Journal of Climate, NPJ Climate and Atmospheric Science, Environmental Research Letters, and Journal of Hydrology.

His contribution to technological innovation is particularly noteworthy. Dr. Hagan has developed high-resolution global drought-monitoring data for scientific and operational applications; contributed to advanced satellite soil-moisture data assimilation systems; developed causal frameworks for predicting floods, droughts, and land-induced heatwaves; and developed long-term environmental datasets that improve our understanding of water and energy exchanges within the climate system. He has also obtained two patents for algorithms developed for causality and extreme-climate evaluation, demonstrating that his work extends beyond academic theory into technological innovation.

The societal relevance of this work is substantial. His research on drought, soil moisture, evapotranspiration, hydro-climatic extremes, and climate impacts provides critical scientific evidence for anticipating and managing risks to water resources, agriculture, and communities. His research has included significant contributions to understanding drought and future climate conditions in Africa, including studies of drought characteristics and evapotranspiration across Sub-Saharan Africa. He has also secured and managed international research funding focused specifically on sustainable water resources and food security in a warming world. Importantly, Dr. Hagan's impact extends beyond publications and inventions. He actively develops the next generation of scientists by supervising graduate researchers across multiple countries, training young scientists, teaching, mentoring, and creating platforms that encourage researchers to connect scientific work with societal needs. Through the Green Living Chats Podcast, he has also helped bring scientists, sustainability practitioners, and broader audiences into conversations about environmental challenges and solutions.

His trajectory from Ghanaian student to internationally recognised hydro-climate scientist, inventor, educator, and research leader makes him an outstanding candidate for the Science, Technology and Innovation Award. Dr. Hagan exemplifies how scientific excellence can transcend borders and disciplines to generate new knowledge, innovative technologies, and practical approaches to challenges affecting humanity.

For his exceptional contributions to scientific research, technological innovation, climate and environmental intelligence, and the development of solutions relevant to water and food security, Dr. Daniel Fiifi Tawia Hagan is highly deserving of the Science, Technology and Innovation Award.

Nomination of Frank Ivan Adama Tackie (FGIP)

Urban and Infrastructure Planner, Chief Executive Officer, The Consortium (CIHSD)

Mfantsipim Old Boy, MOBA '67

Category: Distinguished Business and Entrepreneurship Award

Overview

Mr Frank Ivan Adama Tackie is one of Ghana's most accomplished urban and infrastructure planners, with four decades of professional practice spanning more than 20 countries across Africa, Asia, and the Caribbean. He is the founder and Chief Executive Officer of The Consortium for Innovations in Human Settlements Development (CIHSD), a multi-disciplinary firm of architects, town planners, and engineers based in Accra, and its subsidiary, Comptran Engineering. A proud old student of Mfantsipim School (MOBA '67), he has combined a distinguished national and international planning career with sustained, hands-on commitment to the development of his alma mater.

Education and Professional Standing

Mr Tackie holds an MPhil in Housing from the University of Newcastle Upon Tyne, England. He began his career with a six-year assignment at the United Nations Centre for Human Settlements (UN-Habitat) in Nairobi, Kenya, where he worked on building and infrastructure projects across roughly 25 countries in Africa, Asia, and the Caribbean — an early international grounding that shaped the pan-African outlook of his later career.

Recognitions

He is a Fellow of the Ghana Institute of Planners (FGIP) and served as President of the Institute from 2001 to 2008, leading the professional body that has represented Ghana's planning community since 1969 and helping set national standards for planning practice.

Leadership

Since founding The Consortium in October 1989, Mr Tackie has served as CEO for over 35 years, directly managing more than 150 projects across the built environment. His clients have included major multilateral and bilateral development agencies — among them the World Bank, USAID, GTZ (now GIZ), the Agence Française de Développement (AFD), the African Development Bank (ADB), and UN-Habitat — reflecting the international trust placed in his firm's technical leadership.

Impact

At the national level, Mr Tackie has been engaged in preparing simplified Land Use and Infrastructure Plans for 12 secondary cities across Ghana under the World Bank's Urban 3 Project. He was involved in the master planning, infrastructure development, and securing funding and an anchor developer for the Legon City Project. He prepared a master plan to regenerate Sekondi-Takoradi into an Oil City, funded by Tullow Oil. He was also involved in the Multi-Storey Car Park Project for City Car Park Ltd on High Street, Accra, delivered through Comptran Engineering and other road and infrastructure development projects.

At the regional and international level, Mr Tackie's four-decade career — spanning UN-Habitat assignments and CIHSD-led consultancies — has carried Ghanaian planning expertise into urban and human-settlements projects across more than 20 countries in Africa, Asia, and the Caribbean, in partnership with agencies such as the World Bank, USAID, GTZ/GIZ, AFD, ADB, and UN-Habitat. This body of work has included planning, housing, and infrastructure engagements across the West and East African sub-regions, including Sierra Leone and Uganda, among the countries in which The Consortium has undertaken assignments.

Contributions to Mfantsipim

At a landmark 2008 gathering of Mfantsipim old boys at the Accra National Theatre, Mr Tackie presented the vision and master plan for the School's development, introducing "The Mfantsipim Manifesto: A 10-Year Development Agenda," styled "The Renaissance 1."

The Manifesto rested on three pillars: academic excellence ahead of the pack; leadership qualities of discipline and visible Christian values; and an unparalleled environment built for holistic second-cycle education.

As a professional urban and infrastructure planner, he brought direct technical expertise to the School's long-term physical development—applying a career built on master-planning cities to master-planning his alma mater's campus and facilities.

His first attempt to address these issues came in 1996, when MOBA ’67 sought to develop a master plan as its contribution to the 1997 Speech Day. Although that effort was abandoned due to limited interest and cooperation at the time, the idea was revived in 2006 with the full support of the MOBA’67 Year Group. Frank Tackie then drew on his skills in urban design and infrastructure planning, as well as the multidisciplinary capacity of his consultancy firm, The Consortium, to prepare the Mfantsipim Renaissance Plan for presentation at the 2007 Speech and Prize-Giving Day. Mr Tackie bore the full cost of developing the plan.

The plan, which was launched by MOBA National in 2008, introduced a land-use framework that organised the school into academic, student welfare, teacher welfare, and sports zones; coordinated project selection and funding; encouraged pooled support from sponsoring Year Groups for larger initiatives; and promoted a culture of maintenance.

Mr Tackie’s leadership resulted in the Mfantsipim Old Boys Association (MOBA) appointing him as the Lead for Development Projects at the school. The Renaissance model has largely become the blueprint for MOBA projects. The plan is now due for renewal, given the school’s limited land capacity and the need for substantial, coordinated funding.

Mentorship and Social Responsibility

justification:
Frederick Hans Ampiah embodies the enduring values of Mfantsipim through his exceptional contributions to international development, institutional capacity building, and good governance.

Serving in high-level leadership roles, including as the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) Resident Representative, he has continually driven initiatives aimed at strengthening national security frameworks, democratic institutions, and sustainable development.

His career reflects a deep commitment to fostering strategic partnerships between government agencies, civil society organizations, and international stakeholders to advance transparent governance and peacebuilding efforts.

By consistently upholding the "Dwen Hwe Kan" spirit through impactful public service leadership on the global stage, he serves as an inspiring role model and a distinguished alumnus who brings immense honor to the Mfantsipim community.

Mr. Solomon Kweku Afful represents an extraordinary example of dedication, service, adaptability, and quiet excellence in the history of Mfantsipim School. Having joined the teaching staff in 1992 as a Chemistry teacher, he has devoted the greater part of his professional life to the School, serving generations of students and staff in roles that extended far beyond the conventional responsibilities of a classroom teacher.

One of the earliest demonstrations of his commitment came shortly after he joined the School, when the School was still offering A-level Chemistry. At a critical point, students who were dissatisfied with their preparation threatened to leave the School and seek private tuition elsewhere. When the Headmaster at the time, Mr. Dontwi, met with them, the students made it clear that they would remain only if he took responsibility for preparing them for their final examinations. He accepted the challenge and took the students through the required theoretical and practical work. The result was a historic pass rate in Chemistry for the School that year. From then on, he made it a personal mission to ensure that Mfantsipim students were thoroughly prepared for Chemistry practical examinations, equipping them with the knowledge, confidence, and competence to complete practical assessments well within the allotted time.

His contribution to Mfantsipim, however, was never confined to Chemistry. Even before his departure from the School to teach in the United States, he had demonstrated an aptitude for information technology. Recognising his potential, the then Headmaster, Mr. Dontwi, selected him to attend an IT workshop because he believed that he could contribute meaningfully to the School in that emerging area. Following the workshop, he became more involved in supporting the School's IT activities alongside his teaching responsibilities.

He subsequently had the opportunity to travel to the United States to teach through an international teaching programme, where he remained until his return to Mfantsipim in 2007. On his return, the Chemistry Department was already fully staffed, while the IT Department was in need of personnel. He therefore took on the challenge of heading the IT Department, a responsibility he has carried from 2007 to the present, as he completes his final year of service with the Ghana Education Service in 2026.

In that role, he became one of the quiet forces behind the School's growing dependence on digital systems. As Head of IT and IT Coordinator, he worked tirelessly to ensure that essential digital and administrative processes were completed on time. From registering students for WASSCE and maintaining student records to supporting teachers with the entry and compilation of examination results and facilitating the distribution of reports through electronic means, he consistently placed the needs of the School and its students before his own convenience. Many of these responsibilities required long hours and considerable personal sacrifice, including nights spent in the computer laboratory to ensure that deadlines were met.

Yet, remarkably, Mr. Afful’s transition into IT never meant abandoning his first calling as a Chemistry teacher. He continued to support students in Chemistry, including those who struggled academically and had lost confidence in their abilities. Through additional lessons and patient guidance outside regular class hours, he helped students who appeared destined for very poor results make substantial improvements. Students who had previously performed at levels that placed them at risk of failing went on to achieve grades such as B2, B3, and A1 in WASSCE Chemistry. His commitment to students was therefore not simply about teaching content; it was about restoring confidence and helping young people discover that their academic limitations were not necessarily permanent.

His commitment to academic standards also extended beyond his own students. In one WASSCE examination year, he identified what he believed was an error or omission in the Chemistry marking scheme and wrote to the examiner, explaining why marks ought to be awarded for particular answers. This demonstrated the depth of his subject knowledge and, more importantly, his willingness to advocate for fairness and accuracy in the assessment of students.

His influence has also been felt in the achievements of Mfantsipim beyond the classroom. As NSMQ Coordinator, he guided students who went on to win Mfantsipim's first-ever National Science and Mathematics Quiz trophy in 1999. He subsequently played an advisory role in the selection of coordinators who guided the School to its third and fourth trophies in successive years. He also served as patron of the American Field Service (AFS) and the Mfantsipim Robotics and Computer Club, supporting students as they participated in robotics competitions, where the teams consistently placed among the leading contenders.

Perhaps equally significant is the personal influence he has had on the people around him. His guidance was not limited to students. Generations of teachers have regarded him as someone they could approach when they needed professional advice, practical assistance, or simply the perspective of a trusted and experienced colleague. His patience, fatherly counsel, humility, and willingness to help have made him a source of stability for both students and staff.

His career at Mfantsipim can therefore be seen as a demonstration of service without the need for recognition. He has taught Chemistry, led Information Technology, supported academic administration, mentored students, advised colleagues, strengthened extracurricular programmes, and contributed to some of the School's academic and technological achievements. He has adapted to the changing needs of the School without losing sight of his fundamental commitment to teaching and to the development of young people.

For these reasons, he is more than an outstanding teacher; he has been a quiet engine of Mfantsipim's continued growth and resilience. His career embodies the values that Mfantsipim seeks to instil in its students: resilience in the face of challenges, adaptability in changing circumstances, patience in service to others, and integrity in the pursuit of excellence. His story is a powerful reminder that some of the people who leave the deepest marks on an institution do so without seeking the spotlight. He has served Mfantsipim with the consistency, sacrifice, and dedication of a true institutional servant, and his contribution makes him deserving of the Outstanding Teaching Staff Award.

Dr Bernard Kwaku Okai is a highly dedicated Ghanaian obstetrician and gynaecologist whose career has made a meaningful contribution to women’s reproductive health, particularly in areas of reproductive endocrinology and infertility, sexual and reproductive health, family planning, and maternal health.

With more than a decade of experience in obstetrics and gynaecology, Dr Okai has demonstrated a strong commitment to improving access to quality reproductive healthcare for women in Ghana. He is a member of the Ghana College of Physicians and Surgeons and has been a specialist since 2018. His professional work has also extended beyond clinical practice through his role as an external examiner for the Nurses and Midwifery Council, contributing to the training and professional development of midwives responsible for maternal and reproductive healthcare.

His contribution is particularly significant in underserved communities. As part of his leadership at Bawku Presby Hospital, Dr Okai supported the hosting of a Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Ghana (SOGOG) outreach that provided specialist gynaecological surgeries to women in the Upper East Region, including procedures addressing conditions such as pelvic organ prolapse and obstetric fistula. The outreach also provided opportunities for skills transfer and mentorship for health workers in areas where specialist services are often limited.

Dr Okai has also contributed to research addressing important reproductive and maternal health challenges in Ghana. He was a contributing author to a 2023 multicentre study examining pre-eclampsia and associated risk factors among women in Northern Ghana, adding to the evidence base needed to improve the prevention and management of pregnancy complications. His research has continued to focus on infertility and polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) among women in Ghana. A recent multicentre study involving women seeking infertility care in Kumasi examined the prevalence, phenotypes and fertility treatment outcomes associated with PCOS, an important but understudied reproductive health concern in Ghana.

Dr Okai’s combination of clinical service, research, professional education and support for specialist outreach demonstrates a sustained commitment to improving women’s health. His work addresses both immediate healthcare needs and the longer-term need for stronger evidence, skilled health professionals and equitable access to reproductive health services. For these reasons, he is highly deserving of recognition for his contribution to women’s reproductive health in Ghana.

I am very pleased to nominate David Ewusi-Mensah for the Distinguished Environmental Sustainability Award. David and I are fellow Mfantsipim alumni and long-standing friends. We have collaborated on environmental projects and co-host Green Living Chats, his sustainability podcast. These experiences have enabled me to observe his character, discipline and environmental leadership at close range.

For more than a decade, David has translated environmental research into practical public benefit. His work combines water engineering, nature-based solutions, circular-economy policy, scientific research, public education and mentorship. As Lead Consultant on a World Bank PROBLUE assignment, he led nationwide research, stakeholder engagement and the drafting process that contributed to Ghana’s first three national PET standards—GS 1239, GS 1387 and GS 1388. These standards strengthen environmental protection, consumer safety and Ghana’s circular plastics economy.

David’s influence extends internationally. He produced APEC’s 2024 report on world-class circular-economy industrial parks, providing practical guidance to 21 Asia-Pacific economies. His peer-reviewed research advances low-energy desalination, wastewater treatment and African policy responses to microplastic pollution. He has authored or co-authored 22 publications, and his work has received more than 750 citations.

Through Eco Amet Solutions, which he co-founded and leads, David has developed AFRICER as a Pan-African research-to-policy platform. He has promoted ecological constructed wetlands and brought together researchers, policymakers, practitioners and communities to address plastics, biowaste and circularity. His continuing work also addresses water access in Kenya, regenerative urban water systems in Sierra Leone, and flood and watershed resilience in Accra.

As David’s podcast co-host, I have personally witnessed his ability to make complex environmental issues understandable and useful. Green Living Chats has produced more than 100 conversations covering water, sanitation, climate change, circularity, business and human rights; and has been recognized as one of the most influential green-based podcasts. He has also demonstrated a deep commitment to mentoring emerging sustainability leaders.

David exemplifies “Dwen Hwe Kan.” He thinks ahead, connects science with service, and develops systems that protect water, health, livelihoods and ecosystems. I recommend him for this award without reservation.

## Testimonial for Mrs. Constance Ewuraesi Nkrumah Oduro — “Auntie Nurse”

Mrs. **Constance Ewuraesi Nkrumah Oduro**, affectionately known to generations of Mfantsipim students as **“Auntie Nurse,”** was a remarkable woman whose life was defined by compassion, dedication, professional excellence and selfless service. Born on **31 August 1919 in Kaduna, Nigeria**, she trained as a Registered Nurse and later as a midwife, serving with distinction at several hospitals across Ghana before joining Mfantsipim School.

On **8 November 1971**, she was appointed School Nurse by the then Headmaster, **Mr. O. K. Monney**, to take responsibility for the health and welfare of approximately **800 students**. Her appointment was particularly significant given the demands of caring for a large population of young men. Yet, through her gentle, caring and motherly disposition, she rose to the challenge and served the School with exceptional commitment.

For **24 years**, from 1971 to 1995, Auntie Nurse became much more than a healthcare provider. She cared for thousands of boys who passed through Mfantsipim, treating their ailments with patience and kindness and providing reassurance when they were unwell or vulnerable. She also extended her care to members of staff and their families. Her dedication contributed to a reduction in unnecessary hospital visits, thereby easing the burden on the School administration and helping students remain focused on their academic work.

Her relationship with the students went beyond the formal responsibilities of her position. She regarded them as her **grandchildren**, and they, in turn, remembered her with deep affection. Her impact was such that, years after her retirement, the **1983 year group organised a special celebration for her 90th birthday in 2009**, demonstrating the enduring gratitude of those she had cared for.

Auntie Nurse retired from Mfantsipim on **1 September 1995**, having left an indelible mark on the School and on the lives of the thousands of students she served. She remained deeply connected to Mfantsipim until her passing on **5 August 2011**.

**Mrs. Constance “Auntie Nurse” Oduro exemplified the values of service, compassion, duty and love. Her legacy lives on in the countless Mfantsipim students whose lives she touched. This award therefore honours not only her years of service, but the enduring spirit of care and humanity with which she served the Mfantsipim family.**
